findings.title: Django QuerySet does not support negative slicing
findings.body: In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset is negative, the code executes `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with a negative start_offset. Django QuerySets explicitly disallow negative slicing — the __getitem__ implementation raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported.` whenever k.start or k.stop is negative. Every request that takes this branch will crash with 500 instead of paginating. The adjacent comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong; the framework does no such thing.

findings.title: Comment falsely asserts queryset-level permission enforcement
findings.body: The comment 'This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' preceding the negative-offset branch is incorrect. No queryset-level filtering is added in this code path; the same queryset is sliced. If the slice were ever accepted by the ORM, it would let the caller view arbitrary rows beyond the cursor without any extra scoping. The justification does not match the code, and given the surrounding logic, the author appears to have meant it as a permission guarantee that the patch does not actually provide.

findings.title: Permission gate does not match its 'authorized administrators' comment
findings.body: The new branch is gated by `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but the comment immediately above says 'authorized administrators'. `has_global_access` is granted to Sentry staff who can read every org; it does not imply administrative rights in the calling organization. The PR title and comments talk about admins, while the code quietly extends access to any global-access member (e.g., support engineers). Either the comment is wrong or the gate is wrong; the mismatch should be resolved before merging, especially given the buggy 'advanced feature' being enabled.

findings.title: No tests for the optimized-pagination code path
findings.body: The PR introduces a new query parameter (optimized_pagination), a new paginator class (OptimizedCursorPaginator), and a new kwarg (enable_advanced_features) plumbed through self.paginate, but no tests are added for any of these. Given that the underlying behavior crashes due to Django's negative-indexing restriction, the absence of a test is what allowed the bug to ship. A test exercising the new branch (and the negative-offset path it claims to enable) would have caught this immediately.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result
findings.body: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is an almost-verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result (lines 136–215) with only the negative-offset branch swapped in. This duplicates ~70 lines and means any future fix to BasePaginator.get_result (correctness, edge cases, the post_query_filter ordering, the extra-row trimming, etc.) must be re-applied here. If the feature is meant to ship, it should override only the offset calculation (e.g., a small helper) and delegate the rest to super().get_result, or use a flag on BasePaginator itself.

findings.title: Cursor comments claim a behavior change that doesn't exist
findings.body: The added comments in Cursor.__init__ state 'Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios' and 'This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets', but the code is unchanged — `self.offset = int(offset)` already accepted negative ints before this patch. The comments misrepresent a no-op as a deliberate performance/feature change and tie the Cursor abstraction to a feature (negative offsets) that the rest of the system cannot actually consume.
